title: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893
hook: a young monk stands up in Chicago and his first five words are a greeting

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's lizard on the tree: every color, and sometimes no color at all. Did you ask what someone else saw? Today, one of the young men who sat in Ramakrishna's room. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

Chicago. A big hall, a platform crowded with delegates from many religions, each waiting a turn to speak. Among them is a young Hindu monk. In Ramakrishna's room he was called Narendranath. Here he's Swami Vivekananda, and he's a long way from Bengal. When his turn finally comes, he stands up, faces the crowd, and opens not with an argument or a defense of his tradition, but with a greeting. Today, what he said first, and what he said after it.
screen: `CHICAGO.` → `A YOUNG MONK FROM BENGAL.` → `HE OPENS WITH A GREETING.`

segments.voice: The occasion was the World's Parliament of Religions, and his short talk on the opening day is printed in his collected works as the response to the welcome. His first words were: Sisters and Brothers of America. Tradition says the hall broke into applause before he could go on. Whatever the crowd heard in it, the greeting does something simple: it makes strangers into family before a single idea is offered. Then come the ideas. He thanks his listeners in the name of the monks of his order and of the Hindu people. He says his tradition taught him not only to tolerate other paths but to accept them. And he gives two texts to show what he means. The first is a hymn he says he learned as a boy: as rivers rising in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so the different paths people take, crooked or straight, all lead to you, Lord. The second is from the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says, in effect: whoever comes to me, by whatever road, I reach them. Then he names what he hopes is ending: sectarianism, bigotry, and fanaticism, which, he says, have filled the earth with violence. He hopes the bell that rang that morning to open the Parliament will turn out to be their death knell. Notice the shape. A greeting, two old texts, one hope. He didn't arrive with a new teaching. He carried in songs and verses from home, and spoke them where the whole room could hear.
screen: `SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA.` · `NOT ONLY TOLERATE, BUT ACCEPT.` · `RIVERS INTO ONE SEA.` · `A BELL FOR THE END OF FANATICISM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind a room you'll walk into soon: an office, a classroom, a family dinner, a group chat. Picture the people in it, especially the ones who are hard for you. Now, silently, try greeting them the way he greeted Chicago: as sisters and brothers. Don't force a feeling. Just say the words inside and notice what happens in your chest when you get to the difficult faces. If you pray, you can hold that room in a prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Vivekananda. Ramakrishna's disciple, the monk who greeted a hall in Chicago as sisters and brothers before saying anything else.
Your line: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893. Today, the next time you speak to a group, open with something that makes them family before you make your point. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Vivekananda's Chicago addresses are printed in his Complete Works, and Hindu and Vedanta groups read them aloud in study circles and at gatherings.

a warm greeting that calls the audience family.
